name: Nyambo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_quote: If a root bears a stress, that stress will be realized on the initial syllable of the root. ... There is a language-specific prohibition in Kinyambo against a prominence in phrase-final position.
sweep_summary: Nyambo (nyam1277) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Bickmore 1989. All four works with stress in the title are Bickmore or Bickmore-derived. (1) Bickmore 1989, pp.47-53 re-read and pp.50/53 checked against page scan) confirms: roots are stressed or stressless, stress is realized root-initially as H, phrase-final prominence is banned, nine penult exceptions are loans/reduplications. (2) Bickmore 1992 (Phonology 9) remains paywalled (Crossref/OpenAlex/Unpaywall/S2 closed, no author copy on his the Internet Archive-archived UAlbany pages); only the Cambridge 'Extract' (closing paragraph) is open and it asserts multiple phonemic stress levels, consistent with the lexical coding, silent on placement; priority medium. (3) Philippson 1991 thesis (author PDF already held under bemb1257; Nyambo passages extracted to is new to the per-language bibliography: p.500 classifies Nyambo as 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H' with 'H s'associe à la syllabe marquée' and a pre-pausal penult vs contextual final alternation; p.413/487 place it among Rutara languages that reduced tone to accent via Meeussen's rule; second-hand (from Bickmore 1988) and confirms. (4) Bickmore 1990 (Inkelas & Zec volume) is a phrasal-phonology chapter, print-only (Google Books partial preview blocked, no archive.org/HathiTrust copy); priority low. Best statement read remains the catalog's own deciding source (Bickmore 1989 p.50/53); no supersession. discovery used Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE, archive.org, the Google Books feed and the Internet Archive. updated at

new_statements.quote: If a root bears a stress, that stress will be realized on the initial syllable of the root. With the exception of monosyllabic roots and the word a-má-iso 'eyes' (which cases will be discussed below), all the forms in Table I conform to this statement. There are, however, some surface exceptions to this generalization. There are nine cases known to me (out of approximately 380 nouns in my data base) in which a High tone is born by a non-initial mora in a noun root. [...] [p.53] I will assume that monosyllabic roots are like other roots in that some may be stressed and some stressless. There is a language-specific prohibition in Kinyambo against a prominence in phrase-final position.
new_statements.citation: Bickmore, Lee Stephen. 1989. Kinyambo Prosody. PhD dissertation, UCLA, printed p.50 sec.3.3 and p.53 sec.3.5
new_statements.locator: printed p.50 sec.3.3 'The position of underlying prominence' (PDF 68); printed p.53 sec.3.5 (PDF 71)
new_statements.reading: Stress in Kinyambo is a lexical property of roots (some roots stressed, some stressless; Table I p.47 has All-Low nouns at every length), and when a root is stressed the stress is realized on the root-initial syllable, surfacing as a High (or Falling) tone; a ban on phrase-final prominence shifts a monosyllabic root's stress leftward onto the prefix, and nine penult-stressed nouns are Swahili loans or reduplications. Philippson 1991 (p.500, second-hand from Bickmore 1988) independently classifies Nyambo as an accentual language whose H docks on the lexically marked syllable. This supports the catalog's 'lexical' coding exactly; nothing new read in this search of works with stress in the title supersedes it.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction to the classification. One small overstatement in the compiler gloss: the nine penult-H nouns (p.50 ex. 1) are not all "Swahili loans or reduplications" — Bickmore sorts them as three loans (e-barúa, e-zawáadi, e-papái), two or three reduplications (o-ru-huguhúgu, e-ki-zuunguzúungu, possibly e-ki-goongóro), two derived nominalisations (e-ch-akúrya, o-mu-tamíire) and one unexplained (e-ñañíiñi 'star', pp.51-52); fn.4 p.50 puts the exception count at twelve of 620 stems. This does not change the bearing.

tone_statements.citation: Hubbard, Kathleen. 1994. Duration in Moraic Theory. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (advisor Larry M. Hyman). Open access at eScholarship, item 7x252973.
tone_statements.quote: Runyambo and Luganda have very similar two-tone systems (surface High and Low, of which only H is marked here),and both have a grammatical rule that assigns a H tone to the second mora of a verb stem in certain tenses (see section 1.5). … since rising tones are not permitted in either language, a syllable with H tone on the second mora surfaces as all-H. … we can say that the tone bearing unit in these languages is either (1) a strong mora or (2) a weak mora which is uniquely linked to a vowel.
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, High vs Low (only H marked, L by default); the mora is the tone-bearing unit; a grammatical H docks on the 2nd stem mora; no rising tones, falling tones only in the penult; non-stress.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every piece of the deciding text (Bickmore 1989:48, 50, 51, 53) is present verbatim in the scan we hold at the stated sections/pages (PDF = printed + 18), confirmed from the on-disk scanned of those pages; Table I p.47 shows All-Low nouns at all lengths and p.53 states roots may be 'stressed' or 'stressless', which is exactly the basis for coding prominence as a lexical property with root-initial realization. (2) Deciding source: a 229-pp UCLA phonology dissertation (1989) wholly on Kinyambo prosody, fieldwork-based, top of Glottolog's list; its 1992 Phonology article is the same analysis. Nothing later addresses word prominence: France 2021 (downloaded now, open AJOL) is segmental and silent; Hubbard is duration phonetics; Katamba 1991/Odden 1995 are survey chapters.
